newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE-Virginia becomes leading state for executions.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Virginia becomes leading state for executions.

text.p: Death is on a roll in the state of Virginia.

If convicted murderer Coleman Wayne Gray is put to death by lethal injection as scheduled on Feb. 26, he will be the seventh person executed by the state in the past 14 weeks. Spurred by Gov. George Allen, Virginia led the nation last year with eight executions, despite the fact that it is only the 12th largest state in population.

Gray, 39, was convicted of the 1985 murder of shopkeeper Richard McClelland. His last hopes of avoiding execution lie in the U.S. Supreme Court, which rejected an earlier appeal, and a clemency plea to the tough anti-crime governor.

Allen, a Republican with national political ambitions, says the death penalty is an important part of his anti-crime strategy. "The message is that Virginia is enforcing the law. Those who commit violent, premeditated, heinously vile murders can receive the death penalty," he said recently.

Another part of his policy has been the introduction of "truth in sentencing" depriving violent criminals of a chance to gain early release through parole. Parole was ended and stiffer sentences imposed on violent and repeat offenders for crimes committed after Jan. 1 1995. A first-degree murderer can now expect to serve almost 38 years in prison compared to an average of less than 12 1/2 under the old system.

But evidence is growing that juries prefer to send criminals to jail rather than execute them if they are sure the offenders will never be released. Since the sentencing laws changed, eight defendants have been convicted of capital murder in Virginia but only two were sentenced to death, one by a judge. The other six received life without parole.
DEATH PENALTY IS POPULAR
Polls show the death penalty is overwhelmingly popular in the United States, the only Western industrial nation to carry out executions.
Since 1995, Virginia has allowed the condemned a choice of death by electrocution or by lethal injection. There has been only one taker for electrocution and his execution was stayed.
Most executions in Virginia no longer command much public attention. They are covered by newspapers and television stations but they are rarely Page One news.

An exception was Joseph O'Dell, whose case attracted a clemency plea from Pope John Paul II last December. O'Dell, whose appeal is now before the U.S. Supreme Court, even has his own home page on the World Wide Web.
Victims' family members, who are allowed to witness executions, say they bring some closure to their sufferings.

"I'm opposed to capital punishment on moral grounds," said Gail Sztanko, whose son Alex was brutally murdered. But, days before her son's killer, Carl George, was executed this month, she said George was "not a human being" but a merciless beast who had lived a "life without merit." The family chose not to attend the execution.

Virginia's death row is located at Mecklenburg prison in the south of the state. Four days before the scheduled execution, the inmate is transferred to the Greensville Correctional Centre in Jarratt, a few miles away.
FAMILY REUNIONS ON EXECUTION DAY

"During the four days prior to execution, inmates are allowed contact visits with attorneys and non-contact visits with family and clergy. They can place collect telephone calls to family and friends," David Botkins of the Virginia Department of Corrections said.
"On the day of the execution, the inmate is allowed contact visits with immediate family members. All visits must be concluded by 3 p.m. with the exception of lawyers and clergy."
The condemned may request anything from the prison's 28-day menu for his last meal, which is served at 6 p.m. At 7, he is allowed to take a shower.

A team of 12 to 15 correctional officers volunteer for the execution. Each one has an assigned task such as securing the prisoner's limbs, inserting the intravenous drip into his arm or hooking him up to a heart monitor.

Prior to execution, the sentence is read and the prisoner is given the opportunity to make a final statement. These sometimes include sentiments of remorse, as in the case of Ronald Lee Hoke, who said last Dec. 16: "I know I have caused a lot of pain to the victim's family. I hope one day they can forgive me. I love you, to my girlfriend, Dawn."
Lem Tuggle, who was put to death three days before Hoke, told the assembled witnesses "Merry Christmas".
